nameStory: The broad-winged hawk gets its name from its distinctive wing shape - relatively short but notably broad wings that help it soar efficiently through forest openings. When you see one gliding overhead, those wide wings are unmistakable, spreading out like a living sail against the sky.
description: The broad-winged hawk is a medium-sized raptor that's perfectly built for life in New England's forests. About the size of a crow, it has compact proportions with those signature broad wings that taper to somewhat pointed tips. These hawks come in two color variations: a common light morph with brown and white markings, and a darker morph that's mostly brown with less white. Like most raptors, females are noticeably larger than males.

idTips.label: Wing Shape
idTips.description: Broad, relatively short wings that taper to pointed tips - quite different from the longer, narrower wings of other forest hawks

idTips.label: Size Comparison
idTips.description: Crow-sized with compact proportions - smaller and stockier than red-tailed hawks but larger than sharp-shinned hawks

idTips.label: Color Morphs
idTips.description: Light morph shows brown back and wings with white chest marked by brown barring; dark morph is predominantly brown throughout with minimal white areas

idTips.label: Flight Style
idTips.description: Soars with wings held flat and steady, often circling in thermals - less flapping than accipiters like Cooper's hawks

idTips.label: Tail Pattern
idTips.description: Shows distinct black and white bands across the tail when viewed from below, creating a striped appearance

habitat: Look for broad-winged hawks in mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially areas with openings like clearings, wetlands, or forest edges where they can hunt. They prefer unbroken woodland but need some open spaces within or adjacent to the forest for hunting small mammals, amphibians, and reptiles. During migration, you might spot them soaring over any landscape as they travel in large flocks called 'kettles.'

seasonality.spring: Arriving from Central and South America in April and May, broad-winged hawks are establishing territories and beginning courtship. Listen for their distinctive whistle-like call echoing through the awakening forest.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when they're most likely to be seen and heard. Adults are actively hunting to feed their young and may be more conspicuous as they soar over forest openings.
seasonality.fall: The spectacular migration season! September brings massive flocks or 'kettles' of broad-winged hawks that can number in the thousands as they head south. This is your best chance to see many at once.
seasonality.winter: Almost entirely absent from New England as they winter in the tropics from Mexico to Brazil. Any hawk you see in winter forests is likely a different species.

funFact: Broad-winged hawks create one of nature's most incredible spectacles during fall migration - they gather in massive swirling flocks called 'kettles' that can contain thousands of birds, looking like a living tornado of hawks spiraling up on thermal currents before streaming south together.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with red-shouldered hawks, which share similar forest habitat and size. Remember: broad-winged hawks have broader, more pointed wings and cleaner black-and-white tail bands, while red-shoulders show rusty shoulder patches and more crescent-shaped wing windows when flying.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'buteo' refers to a group of hawks known as 'soaring hawks' because they ride thermals and updrafts rather than relying on rapid wingbeats like the bird-hunting accipiters. This energy-efficient flight style makes their incredible long-distance migrations possible.
compareHints: Compared to its buteo relatives, the broad-winged hawk is the most forest-dependent and migratory. Red-tailed hawks are larger with longer wings and prefer more open country, while red-shouldered hawks have more distinctive rusty coloring and longer tails. Broad-wings are also the only buteo in New England that completely abandons the region in winter.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buteo hawks, red-tails are the largest and bulkiest, while red-shouldered hawks are more slender with distinctive reddish shoulder patches and prefer wooded areas.
Among buteo hawks in New England, red-shouldered hawks are the forest specialists with the most distinctive barring pattern.
Unlike the year-round resident Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Rough-legged Hawks are strictly winter visitors from the Arctic.
Compared to our common Red-tailed and Red-shouldered Hawks, Swainson's Hawks have longer, more pointed wings and are built more for long-distance soaring.
Ferruginous hawks absolutely dwarf their buteo relatives – they're significantly larger than red-tailed hawks with much broader wings and a more massive build.
